title: Addition with Regrouping Grade 2: The Column Method Made Clear + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach addition with regrouping in Grade 2 the written way: line up columns, add the ones, carry the ten. Clear steps, common-mistake fixes and a free quiz.
excerpt: Carrying trips up more Grade 2 children than any other part of addition. Here is the column method, step by step, why we carry at all, and the two mistakes to watch for — plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 27 + 8 on a page and ask a Grade 2 child to solve it in a column, and here is what usually happens: they add the 7 and the 8, get 15, and write all of 15 under the ones. Now the answer reads 315. That single moment — where fifteen ones will not fit in the ones column — is the whole of addition with regrouping in Grade 2. Get a child over that hump and the rest is practice. Miss it and every three-digit sum for the next two years wobbles.

This post is about the written column method — lining numbers up, adding column by column, and carrying. It is not about mental tricks like adding on in your head; a separate lesson owns those. Here we want a child who can pick up a pencil, set out 148 + 76 neatly, and get 224 every single time.

What regrouping actually means

Regrouping (older books call it carrying) rests on one fact from place value: ten ones make one ten, and ten tens make one hundred. When a column adds up to 10 or more, the digits cannot all stay in that column — a place only holds one digit, 0 to 9. So we swap ten of the smaller units for one of the next unit up and move it left. Fifteen ones become one ten and five ones. The 5 stays; the 1 travels to the tens column. That is it. Everything else is bookkeeping.

I labour this point with counters or a ten-frame before any pencil work, because a child who has physically traded ten loose beans for one stick of ten never forgets why the little 1 goes on top. Children who only memorise ‘put the 1 up there’ forget it under pressure.

The column method, step by step

Take 148 + 76. Set it out with ones under ones, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds. The numbers are different lengths, so the 76 shifts right to sit against the right edge.

StepWhat you doCarry
Ones8 + 6 = 14. Write 4, carry 1 ten.1 above the tens
Tens4 + 7 + 1 (carried) = 12 tens. Write 2, carry 1 hundred.1 above the hundreds
Hundreds1 + 0 + 1 (carried) = 2. Write 2.none

Read the answer off the bottom: 224. Notice the order — you always start at the right, in the ones, and move left. Starting from the left is the single most common wrong instinct, and it breaks the carrying.

Why we go right to left

You carry into a column, so you have to finish the column on its right before you know what to add. Add the tens before the ones and you would not yet know whether a 1 is coming across. Right to left keeps every carry arriving before it is needed.

The classic mistakes — and how to fix them

In my experience teaching seven-year-olds, almost every regrouping error is one of a small handful. Here is what to watch for at the kitchen table.

  • Forgetting to carry. The child adds 8 + 6, writes 4, and simply drops the ten. Fix: make them say the full number out loud — ‘fourteen, so four down and one up’ — every time, until the carry is a habit, not an afterthought.
  • Writing the whole two-digit sum. The 315 mistake from the opening. Fix: one box per digit. Squared paper, or drawn boxes, physically stops a child cramming 15 into one square.
  • Mis-aligning the columns. Lining 148 and 76 up on the left, so the 7 sits under the 1. Everything downstream is wrong. Fix: always start writing from the right-hand edge; on squared paper, one digit per square lines the places up for you.
  • Adding the carried 1 in the wrong place. Some children add the carried 1 back into the ones instead of the tens. Fix: write the small 1 at the top of the next column so it is visually parked where it belongs.
  • Forgetting the final carry. On sums like 90 + 80, the tens make 17, and children write 170 fine — but on 950 + 80 the last carry into the hundreds gets dropped. Fix: remind them the leftmost column can still overflow.

When does a Grade 2 child need this?

By NCERT expectations, Grade 2 covers addition of two- and three-digit numbers with regrouping. A fair sequence is: two-digit sums that cross once (like 27 + 8, then 46 + 38), then three-digit sums that carry in the ones only, then sums that carry twice (148 + 76). Do not jump to double carries until single carries are boring. Boring is the goal here — boring means fluent.

One honest caveat: neat handwriting matters more than usual with this topic. A child whose columns drift will make alignment errors no matter how well they understand the maths. Squared paper is not babyish; I still recommend it right through the year.

A quick worked check

Try 265 + 158 together. Ones: 5 + 8 = 13, write 3, carry 1. Tens: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12, write 2, carry 1. Hundreds: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Answer 423. If your child gets 313 or 413, you have just found exactly which carry they dropped — and that is the most useful thing a practice sum can tell you.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Addition with Regrouping Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on column addition with carrying. Work each one in a column on paper, pick your answer, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Add the ones: 7 + 8 = 15. Write 5, carry 1 ten. Tens: 2 + 1 = 3. Answer 35.

questions.q: In the ones column you add 9 + 6 = 15. What do you write in the ones place, and what do you carry?
questions.explanation: Ten ones make one ten. Fifteen ones are one ten and five ones: write 5, carry the 1 ten.

questions.q: Which column should you always add first?
questions.explanation: Start at the right, in the ones, and move left, so each carry arrives before you need it.
Ones: 8 + 6 = 14, write 4 carry 1. Tens: 4 + 7 + 1 = 12, write 2 carry 1. Hundreds: 1 + 1 = 2. Answer 224.

questions.q: Why do we carry a 1 to the next column?
options: To make the sum look neat
Because ten ones make one ten
questions.explanation: A place only holds one digit. Ten ones are traded for one ten, which moves left to the tens column.

questions.q: A child writes 27 + 8 as the answer 315. What went wrong?
options: They lined up the columns wrong
They wrote all of 15 in the ones instead of carrying
questions.explanation: 7 + 8 = 15. They should write 5 and carry 1. Cramming 15 into the ones gives the wrong 315.
Ones: 5 + 8 = 13, write 3 carry 1. Tens: 6 + 5 + 1 = 12, write 2 carry 1. Hundreds: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Answer 423.

faq.q: What is regrouping in Grade 2 addition?
faq.a: Regrouping, also called carrying, is what you do when a column adds to 10 or more. You keep the ones digit in that column and carry the ten (or hundred) to the next column left, because ten ones make one ten.

faq.q: Why do we add from right to left?
faq.a: Because carries travel leftward. You finish the ones before you know what carries into the tens, so starting on the right means every carried 1 arrives just before you need to add it in.

faq.q: My child keeps forgetting to carry. What helps?
faq.a: Have them say the full number out loud — ‘fourteen, so four down and one up’ — for every column. Squared paper with one digit per box also stops them cramming a two-digit sum into one place.

faq.q: At what stage should Grade 2 children learn regrouping?
faq.a: After they are secure with sums that do not cross ten. Start with two-digit sums that carry once, then three-digit sums, and only move to double carries once single carries feel easy.
